title: India's Own Attorney General Called E20 Fuel an 'Experiment.' The Government Spent the Next 48 Hours in Damage Control.
excerpt: A viral courtroom video has turned simmering consumer anger over mandatory ethanol-blended petrol into the Modi government's biggest domestic headache this summer.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India's attorney general called E20 fuel an 'experiment,' igniting public outrage.
  • Mandatory E20 fuel has led to complaints of reduced efficiency and engine damage.
  • The government defends E20, citing minimal mileage reduction of 2-3%.
  • Public anger stems from loss of choice in fuel options for vehicles.
  • E20 controversy poses risks for India's auto sector and diaspora investments.

India's attorney general called the country's mandatory ethanol-blended fuel an "experiment" in open court this week. A viral video of the remark has since turned what was already simmering consumer frustration into a full-blown political crisis for the Modi government. The controversy centres on E20, a blend of 20 per cent ethanol mixed with petrol that became the only option at nearly all of India's 90,000 fuel stations last year. The government achieved its blending target ahead of schedule, framing it as a clean-energy triumph that cuts crude imports, lowers carbon emissions and boosts farm incomes. But for millions of motorists who no longer have a choice at the pump, the policy has become a source of daily aggravation. ## The 'Experiment' That Went Viral During a Supreme Court hearing on ethanol procurement contracts, Attorney General R. Venkataramani told the bench that E20 was an "experiment" whose results would only come out next year. Video of the remark spread rapidly on social media, racking up hundreds of thousands of views and confirming what many car owners already suspected: the government was not entirely sure this would work. Venkataramani later told Reuters he used the word "experiment" in the narrow context of ethanol supply volumes, not the fuel programme itself. The Ministry of Law and Justice called the media coverage "completely false." But the damage was done. The government's own attorney general had, on camera, used the one word that no policymaker wants associated with a nationwide mandate. ## Motorists Fight Back > **"Venkataramani later told Reuters he used the word "experiment" in the narrow context of ethanol supply volumes, not the fuel programme itself."** The backlash has been building for months. Hundreds of motorists have posted complaints on X alleging reduced fuel efficiency, engine corrosion, and increased wear on car parts. In one video viewed over 500,000 times, a motorist identified as Manish Kashyap stands in a workshop with his car, saying it needed costly repairs after just two months on E20. "I have spent a lot of money on this car and paid taxes only to find that after two months my car is not working," he said. Tehseen Poonawalla, a New Delhi-based socialite and Congress supporter, announced plans for a protest against the E20 policy in the capital on Sunday, claiming thousands had expressed interest. Opposition Congress minister Priyank Kharge said on X that the government "cannot challenge citizens to prove damage when your own data is still pending." Some of the claims circulating online have veered into the absurd — one viral post alleged that ants and bees are attracted to fuel caps because ethanol contains sugar. Bharat Petroleum dismissed that claim, explaining that fuel-grade ethanol undergoes fermentation and distillation that eliminate residual sugars. ## The Government's Defence
Public Response to E20 Fuel
›Motorists report engine corrosion and costly repairs.
›Protests planned against E20 policy in New Delhi.
›Claims of fuel attracting insects dismissed by Bharat Petroleum.
›Social media campaign labeled as 'fear-mongering' by government.
Petroleum Minister Hardeep Singh Puri pushed back, comparing E20 to fuel used in motor racing. "They use it in racing cars also, the acceleration increases. Mileage, yes, it may drop a little," he said. The ministry released a 15-page factsheet calling the social media campaign "fear-mongering" built on "false, baseless, scientifically unfounded" claims. The government points to studies by the Automotive Research Association of India (ARAI) and the Society of Indian Automobile Manufacturers (SIAM) showing that the actual mileage reduction from E20 is about 2 to 3 per cent — not the 20 to 30 per cent that some influencers claim. SIAM has confirmed that warranty coverage remains valid for vehicles running E20. Insurance companies have issued similar clarifications. But the core of the public anger is not about data — it is about choice. Older blends like E5 and E10, seen as more compatible with ageing vehicles, have been pulled from nearly every station in the country. Two fuel station managers in Lucknow told Reuters that drivers were so angry that some stations had stopped even mentioning the change. ## What This Means for the Diaspora For NRIs who visit India regularly, the E20 controversy touches a practical nerve. Anyone renting a car or driving a family vehicle during trips home is filling up with the same fuel that has sparked complaints about reduced mileage and engine trouble — particularly in older vehicles that many Indian families still rely on.
Government's Stance on E20
›Petroleum Minister compares E20 to racing fuel.
›Government plans to increase ethanol blending to 25% after tests.
›E20 policy remains despite public backlash.
›Warranty coverage for vehicles using E20 confirmed.
The broader implications are economic. India's auto sector, a major draw for diaspora investment, is already battling slower sales and shortages of rare-earth magnets. Consumer backlash against a government fuel mandate adds another layer of uncertainty for an industry that produces over four million passenger vehicles a year. The government has signalled it will not reverse course. Puri said India would consider moving to 25 per cent ethanol blending only after completing additional tests. "India's ethanol journey is unstoppable," he said. For now, 1.4 billion Indians have no choice but to agree.
